newsitem.title: INDIA: New India Congress party boss a shrewd tactician.
newsitem.headline: New India Congress party boss a shrewd tactician.

text.p: For years, Sitaram Kesri was known as "Mr. Moneybags" for his ability to raise funds at will for India's Congress party while keeping his own finances immaculately clean.
Now, his election as Congress president in September and as the party's parliamentary boss on Friday has propelled the self-effacing backroom strategist to the forefront of national politics.

"Age is not with me," the veteran party official lamented to Reuters just last week, his apparent humility belying the toughness needed for a rough inner party campaign to become the Congress Parliamentary Party's (CPP) powerful leader.
"I need the support of the younger lot. There is so much to be done."
As the new CPP leader, Kesri will indeed have much on his plate, including rebuilding the party from its worst-ever defeat in general elections last year.
Kesri's unanimous selection by "consensus", without a formal vote, came about in much the same controversial way as the exit of his predecessor, former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao.
"We want an election, not a fraud in the name of consensus," Kesri's main rival for the CPP job, former minister Rajesh Pilot, was heard saying in the party office this week.

Some newspapers speculated over a possible split, saying Rao, who was forced to resign from the two posts now occupied by Kesri after criminal charges of forgery and cheating were filed against him, could lead a breakaway group.
But Kesri prevailed on Friday as Pilot quietly withdrew his candidacy in the face of strong opposition.
"People who talk about splits do not understand the Congress," Kesri said recently. "It is like a large family in which differences are sorted out collectively."
His philosophical approach has won Kesri the sobriquet of Chacha, or Uncle, among his followers and foes.

"I owe my life to Narasimha Rao," he used to say, referring to the close support Rao gave him when he underwent heart surgery in the United States three years ago. In September, it was Rao who proposed Kesri name as provisional Congress president.
Kesri who speaks faltering English and rustic-accented Hindi, is a party veteran who was jailed many times during India's struggle for independence.
He was a staunch follower of Mahatma Gandhi and has a stature that inspires awe even among senior Congressmen.
As a student, Kesri, who comes from the mineral-rich but economically backward state of Bihar, quit his studies to join the independence movement.
Jailed by the British, he refused parole to attend his father's funeral.
Many believe Kesri's roots in the movement and his amiable disposition could help him bind together the party that led India to freedom but now finds its support dwindling.

In a party which rivals say is too strongly oriented towards the Hindu upper castes and the rich, Kesri has been an outspoken supporter of job quotas in government to help lower castes. He also champions protection for minority Moslems.
Kesri has been the party's treasurer since 1979, and has raised funds for the Congress to fight four general elections.
As a backroom strategist, he has also worked closely with party chiefs and prime ministers of differing styles, from the imperious Indira Gandhi to her impatient son Rajiv and the taciturn Rao.
Kesri was a minister under all three.
